unit_label: Module A: International Banking - Exchange Rates and Forex Business

facts.statement: The foreign exchange market is a communication-system-based market without physical boundaries that operates round the clock across time zones; its participants range from individuals and businesses to commercial and investment banks, central banks, funds and speculators.
facts.locator: Printed p. 5, heading Foreign exchange Markets

facts.statement: Geographically the market runs from Tokyo and Sydney in the east through Hong Kong, Singapore, India, Bahrain, Frankfurt, London and Paris to New York in the west.
facts.locator: Printed p. 5, heading Foreign exchange Markets

facts.statement: Roles of the major participants: central banks manage their reserves and use the market to reduce volatility in the value of the home currency; commercial banks exchange currencies for clients, hedge and invest their own assets and liabilities, and also take views on rates; investment funds and banks move funds between countries for investment and hedging; brokers act as middlemen; corporations move funds for investment or trade; individuals use the market for investment, trade, personal and travel needs.
facts.locator: Printed p. 5, list of major participants

facts.statement: Forex markets usually operate Monday to Friday, and the bulk of trading is over the counter, concluded by telephone or electronic systems.
facts.locator: Printed p. 6, heading Foreign exchange Markets (continued)

facts.statement: Major banks act as market makers by offering two-way (buy and sell) quotes and leaving the caller to choose, which gives the market depth and volume.
facts.locator: Printed p. 6, heading Foreign exchange Markets (continued)

facts.statement: Forward rate = spot rate + premium (or − discount). A currency is at a premium when its forward value is higher than its spot value and at a discount when it is lower; when one currency of a pair is at a premium the other is at a discount.
facts.locator: Printed p. 10, heading Forward Margins - Premium and Discounts

facts.statement: Forward premium and discount are generally determined by the interest rate differential between the two currencies and by future demand and supply; a forward rate so worked out is an expectation, not a guarantee of the future trend.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 10-11, heading Forward Margins - Premium and Discounts

facts.statement: When a currency pair is not quoted directly, its rate is obtained as a cross rate from two quotes that share a common currency, by multiplying them; for example GBP/INR from GBP/USD and USD/INR.

Fixing the rate between two currencies through a third currency is called the chain rule and the result is the cross rate; in the Indian market straight rates are available only for USD/INR, so rates of other currencies against the rupee are derived as cross rates.
In a two-way quote the quoting bank buys at the first figure (bid) and sells at the second (offer).
facts.locator: Printed p. 12, heading Bid and Offer Rates

payload.title: Who is in the forex market, and what each is there for
payload.core_explanation_md:
The foreign exchange market has no building. It is a web of dealing rooms and screens that passes business from centre to centre round the clock, Monday to Friday: Tokyo and Sydney first, then Singapore, India and the Gulf, then Frankfurt and London, and New York last. Most deals are struck over the counter, by phone or on electronic platforms.

Three kinds of player meet there:

- **The steerer.** A central bank manages the country's reserves and steps in to calm swings in its own currency.
- **The price makers and go-betweens.** Large commercial banks quote a buying and a selling rate at the same time, deal for customers and for their own books, and take views on rates. Brokers act as middlemen between the others.
- **The users.** Investment funds, companies and individuals come for a reason outside the market: investing abroad, hedging, paying for trade, travel.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Why does it matter who is on the other side? Because the motive tells you how to read the move. A bank that quotes both sides all day gives the market its depth: a caller can deal either way at once. A central bank dealing in size is usually not chasing a profit; it is smoothing the value of the home currency.

payload.title: Forward rate from spot rate and forward margin
payload.core_explanation_md:
A forward rate is built, not guessed: take today's spot rate and adjust it by the forward margin for the period. If the foreign currency costs more for future delivery than for spot, it is at a **premium** and the margin is added. If it costs less, it is at a **discount** and the margin is subtracted.

The two currencies of a pair always mirror each other: when the dollar is at a premium against the rupee, the rupee is at a discount against the dollar.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: What sets the margin? Mainly the gap between interest rates in the two currencies, together with expected demand and supply for them. So a forward rate is an expectation written into today's prices. It is not a promise about where the spot rate will stand on that date.

variables.name: Forward rate
variables.unit: home currency per unit of foreign currency

variables.name: Spot rate
variables.unit: home currency per unit of foreign currency

variables.name: Forward margin: positive for a premium, negative for a discount

assumptions: Direct quotation: home currency per unit of foreign currency.
The spot rate and the margin are for the same side of the quote, buying or selling.
The margin is for the same period as the forward contract.
common_errors: Adding a discount instead of subtracting it.
Adding a margin quoted in paise or pips to a rate in rupees without converting it first.
Forgetting that a premium on one currency of the pair is a discount on the other.

self_check.prompt_text: Spot USD/INR is 83.40 and the dollar is at a three-month discount of 30 paise (illustrative figures). What is the three-month forward rate, and which currency is at a premium?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 83.10: the discount is subtracted, 83.40 − 0.30. With the dollar at a discount, the rupee is at a premium.

payload.title: No EUR/INR quote on the screen: an exporter's rate by the chain rule
payload.core_explanation_md: In India a straight interbank quote exists for USD/INR; other currencies reach the rupee through the dollar. Illustrative case: a Coimbatore textile exporter receives EUR 25,000. The dealer sees EUR/USD 1.0836/1.0841 and USD/INR 83.4125/83.4175. What interbank EUR/INR rate does the bank start from, before its own margin?

worked_steps.description: Follow the money. The bank buys euros from the exporter, so to square itself it sells those euros for dollars: the market buys euros at its bid.
It then sells the dollars for rupees: the market buys dollars at its bid.
Chain the two so that the dollar cancels.
Rupees for the exporter at that rate, before the bank's margin.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Interbank EUR/INR buying rate ₹90.3858 per EUR; EUR 25,000 is worth ₹22,59,645.00 before margin

self_check.prompt_text: For the exporter's euros, why are both legs taken at the bid, and what would change for an importer who needs euros?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The bank is selling in both legs (euros for dollars, then dollars for rupees), and the market buys at its bid each time. For an importer the bank buys in both legs, so both legs are taken at the offer.

payload.stem_md: The rupee swings sharply within an hour of trading. One participant sells dollars from the country's reserves, not to earn a profit but to steady the rate. Which participant is acting in its expected role?

options.text_md: A commercial bank quoting two-way prices to callers
options.explanation_md: A market-making bank gives the market depth by quoting both sides; steadying the currency from reserves is not its role.

options.text_md: A forex broker matching a buyer with a seller
options.explanation_md: A broker is a middleman between other participants and holds no national reserves.
A central bank manages the reserves and uses the market to reduce volatility in the value of the home currency.

options.text_md: A company covering an import payment
options.explanation_md: A company comes to the market for its own trade or investment needs, not to steady the exchange rate.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Managing the reserves and intervening to smooth the value of the home currency is the central bank's part in the market. The other three deal for customers, for commission or for their own commercial needs.

payload.stem_md: A dealer's screen shows the interbank selling rate for USD/INR at 83.4175 for spot and 84.6325 for delivery in six months (illustrative figures). By how many paise per dollar is the dollar at a forward premium for six months?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the premium in paise to 2 decimal places.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Forward rate = spot rate + premium, so the premium is the forward rate less the spot rate: 84.6325 − 83.4175 = 1.2150 rupees, which is 121.50 paise. The dollar costs more for future delivery, so it is at a premium (and the rupee at a discount).

payload.stem_md: A dealer has EUR/USD 1.0836/1.0841 and USD/INR 83.4125/83.4175 (illustrative figures) and must make a two-way EUR/INR price through the dollar. Take each derived EUR/INR rate to 4 decimal places. What is the spread between the bank's EUR/INR buying and selling rates, in paise?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Round each derived rate to 4 decimal places first, then give the spread in paise to 2 decimal places.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Buying rate: both legs at the bid, 1.0836 × 83.4125 = 90.385785, taken as 90.3858. Selling rate: both legs at the offer, 1.0841 × 83.4175 = 90.43291175, taken as 90.4329. Spread = 90.4329 − 90.3858 = 0.0471 rupees = 4.71 paise. Mixing a bid with an offer gives neither of the bank's rates.
